title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family and the people around you, saying whose is whose.
intro:
Family is at the heart of life in Pakistan, and Urdu has a precise word for every relative: your father's brother is not the same 'uncle' as your mother's brother. In this unit you'll learn the core family words and how to say 'my', 'your' and 'X's'.

You'll also meet the most important fact of Urdu grammar: **every noun is masculine or feminine**, and words that describe or possess it change to match.

grammar.title: Masculine and feminine nouns; plurals
grammar.body:
Every Urdu noun is **masculine** or **feminine**. For people it follows natural gender; for things you must learn it with the word. A useful rule of thumb:

Nouns ending in **-ā** (ا / ہ) are usually masculine: لڑکا boy, بچہ child, کمرہ room.
Nouns ending in **-ī** (ی) are usually feminine: لڑکی girl, بیٹی daughter, کرسی chair.
(There are exceptions: آدمی man, پانی water are masculine.)

**Plurals** (direct case):
Masc. in -ā → -e: لڑکا → لڑکے, بچہ → بچے
Other masc. → no change: آدمی → آدمی, بھائی → بھائی
Fem. in -ī → -iyāṃ: لڑکی → لڑکیاں, بیٹی → بیٹیاں
Other fem. → -eṃ: عورت → عورتیں, بہن → بہنیں

grammar.title: Possession: میرا, آپ کا and the postposition کا / کی / کے
grammar.body:
'Of' is the postposition **کا** kā, and it agrees with the thing possessed (not the owner!), like an adjective:

**کا** before a masculine singular noun
**کی** before a feminine noun (singular or plural)
**کے** before a masculine plural noun (or a respectful singular)

So 'Ali's brother' = علی کا بھائی, 'Ali's sister' = علی کی بہن, 'Ali's brothers' = علی کے بھائی.

The possessive pronouns work the same way: میرا / میری / میرے 'my', ہمارا / ہماری / ہمارے 'our', تمہارا / تمہاری / تمہارے 'your (familiar)', تیرا 'your (intimate)', and for آپ, اس us 'him/her' and ان un 'them' you simply add کا: آپ کا، اس کا، ان کا.

Urdu has no verb 'to have' for family: 'I have two sisters' = **میری دو بہنیں ہیں** 'my two sisters are'.

culture: Pakistani families are often large and close-knit, with grandparents, uncles and cousins living together or nearby. Kinship words are used as polite titles for non-relatives: an older man may be called انکل or چچا, a woman خالہ or آنٹی, a peer بھائی or باجی (older sister). Cousins are often called 'cousin brother/sister' in English and simply بھائی / بہن in Urdu. When complimenting children or good fortune, people say ماشاء اللہ to ward off the evil eye.
